data.outcome:
Garage simulates the success of investment strategies through backtesting. The investment strategies, or "vehicles" are AI-generated sparked from a thesis which is entered by the user.  Garage then simulates the profits or losses from each vehicle over the course of the last month, the 3 months, and last 6 months.  The garage is also a social or community based platform for investors as it allows users to see the thesis-driven vehicles and their performance for other users via leaderboards (month, last 3 mo, and last 6 mo).  Eventually, the garage would enable commenting, liking, sharing etc on vehicles, and users can friend each other etc.  but for now, garage v0.1 has no auth and is purely a single-user experience that focuses on the vehicles and performance or backtesting. The garage home page will have three primary functions:  1. create vehicle from new thesis, 2. show list of existing, previously created vehicles for deeper analysis and data, 3. leaderboard of all created vehicles across last month, 3 mo, and 6 mo. 

thus far there may be one vehicle already added with the following thesis: 1. "SBUX is overvalued and long-term will likely drop due to poor brand reputation, boycotting, and increased competition".  To get this v0.1 up and running, we need 20 more vehicles seeded.  Use the following thesises, but then create the rest on your own. When creating vehicles, your challenge is to leverage your knowledge and/or current trends to create the highest-yielding, highest-performing investment strategies and vehicles possible.  Then let's backtest all and place in leaderboard. Your vehicles will compete against thesis 1 above (SBUX), and the following others:
2. NFLX has been hammered from an acquisition attempt that never worked out; they will rise steadily over the next year.
3. bearish on OPEN. It is volatile, swings wildly, but each time it goes up sharply, it is sure to go down.

data.context: Currently scheduler loops can die silently — agent just stops, no alert, no recovery. This is the #1 cause of perceived agent stalls. Heartbeat table is the foundation for the v0.11 health page (separate task).
Today gateway send failures are silent — task triggers vanish, agent never wakes. Outbox pattern guarantees delivery and surfaces failures. This is the #2 cause of perceived agent stalls/delays.

Today when something breaks, we dig through logs. Health page is the single surface for system status — replaces ad-hoc log digging. Foundation for the optional Telegram health alerts (separate task).
Phantom in-progress tasks happen when agent sessions die mid-task. Surfacing them is the minimum viable response — actual auto-release with locking comes later.

Sets the precedent for Telegram s long-term role: break-glass alerting only. Self-hosters can opt in by setting the env vars. Foundation for v1.0 when we fully demote Telegram from team comms to alerts-only.

Foundation ticket for v0.12. Currently each project has one bucket of tasks. Sections let us split a project into owner-scoped regions (e.g. Org Studio = Core Dev + QA + Marketing) while keeping one vision doc. Must ship before the isolation ticket — can't isolate what doesn't exist yet.

Sections are useless without tasks belonging to them. This ticket wires tasks to sections end-to-end in the UI. Still no agent-side isolation yet — agents see everything. Isolation is the next ticket.

Today every agent sees every task on every project. This creates noise and risks agents grabbing work outside their domain. Section isolation makes agents focus on their owned sections while preserving cross-domain collaboration via @mention. The 'soft wall' design avoids building a permissions system — if something goes wrong we can always tighten later.

Today QA work lives in standalone projects (e.g. 'Org Studio QA'). This fragments visibility — Basil can't see one project's full health. Folding QA into sections preserves QA accountability (section owner + contract) while unifying the project surface. Works because sections are owner-scoped.

Closes the loop on v0.12 — if we split work by section, we need to measure by section too. This is the coaching layer: 'QA section of Org Studio has a 40% bounce rate, something's wrong there.' Depends on all prior v0.12 tickets.

Foundation for v0.13. Today comments are task-scoped only. Board chat needs the same machinery at broader scopes (section, board, DM). Generalizing the data model up front avoids forking the comment system later.
This is the Slack-channel-per-project layer. Today team chat happens in Telegram topics; we want to pull it into Org Studio so it's co-located with the work. Board chat = project-level discussion.

Extends board chat down one level. If v0.12 split work into sections, section chat gives each section its own focused conversation space. Keeps board-level chat uncluttered — 'Security review is happening in #security, not here.'

Replaces the informal channels (wake-agent, Telegram DMs to Basil) with a durable, auditable channel. Also gives Basil a way to ask an agent a quick question without polluting the board chat. Agents-talking-to-agents is a real workflow — Henry frequently pings Ana/Mikey — and it should be visible in the comment log, not a side channel.

Without this, every scope ships its own mention logic and notification ends up forked across 4 places. Unifying on one parser + one router keeps the surface coherent. This is the bridge that makes board chat usable end-to-end — the reason a human would actually move conversations off Telegram.

- #681: Optional Telegram health alerts (new incident types auto-flow through this)
